issues.legal_issue: A transfer of disputed property made after institution of a specific performance suit is subordinate to the rights determined in that suit, even when the transferee purchased in good faith for value without notice.
material_facts: A suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell the property was filed before the owner transferred the property to a second purchaser.
The second purchaser paid value and was found to have acted in good faith without notice of the agreement to sell.
The second purchaser’s transfer occurred while the specific performance suit was pending.
issues.conclusion: The principle of lis pendens applied, and the later transfer could not override the rights established by the decree for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the principle of lis pendens: a transfer during pending litigation does not annul the conveyance but makes it subservient to the rights determined in the litigation, irrespective of the transferee’s notice or good faith. The Court relied on Bellamy v. Sabine, Faiyaz Husain Khan v. Munshi Prag Narain, the Full Bench decision in Smt. Ram Peary v. Gauri, and R.K. Mohammed Ubaidullah v. Hajee C. Abdul Wahab. Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 does not enable a later transfer made during the pending suit to prevail over the operation of lis pendens.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.transfer_during_pending_suit: The owner transferred the property to another person while that suit was pending.
predicates.property_is_subject_of_suit: The transferred property was the property whose rights were being litigated in the suit.

issues.definition: When an enforcement suit concerns property and the owner transfers that property while the suit is pending, the later transfer remains subordinate to the rights determined in the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser who is a defendant in a specific performance suit may raise the plaintiff’s failure to establish readiness and willingness, but the requirement is met where the plaintiff pleaded readiness and willingness and the defendants did not specifically deny it.
material_facts: The subsequent purchaser was a defendant in the specific performance suit.
The plaintiff pleaded that she had been and remained ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
The defendants did not specifically deny the readiness-and-willingness allegation, and the court found the pleading sufficient.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent purchaser could raise the readiness-and-willingness issue, but the plaintiff had sufficiently pleaded that requirement, so the objection did not defeat the claim for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(a), (b), and (c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 prevents specific performance where the plaintiff fails to meet the statutory requirements, including pleading and proving performance or continuous readiness and willingness. A subsequent purchaser may raise that objection, as recognized in Ram Awadh v. Achhaibar Dubey; the Court also referred to Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh concerning the plaintiff’s readiness-and-willingness obligation and a subsequent purchaser’s ability to defend the purchase.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and subsequent_purchaser_is_defendant and plaintiff_pleaded_readiness and defendants_did_not_specifically_deny_readiness

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_is_defendant: A person who acquired the property after the agreement to sell was joined as a defendant in the enforcement suit.
predicates.plaintiff_pleaded_readiness: The plaintiff alleged that she was ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
predicates.defendants_did_not_specifically_deny_rea: The defendants did not specifically deny the plaintiff’s allegation of readiness and willingness.

issues.definition: In a specific performance suit, when a subsequent purchaser is a defendant and the plaintiff pleads readiness and willingness without a specific denial by the defendants, the requirement is treated as satisfied.
